subtopic: Integrity vs despair (as foreseen by the young)
passage:
Dear Jyoti Dadi,
I've been thinking about Sunday since I got back to the hostel. When you said, "I wish I had fought to finish Class 10 instead of keeping quiet," you laughed afterwards, but your voice didn't.
I want you to know I didn't hear it as "now you must top everything for me." I heard it as a map. You showed me which silence cost you.
So here's what I did this week. I put my name down for the English debate, which terrifies me. I haven't asked Professor Rao about the research project yet, but I will by Friday. Some risks aren't worth it, like skipping sleep for marks. These ones feel like they'll let me sleep well at sixty.
Your granddaughter who talks too much,
Ankita

qa.q: What did Jyoti Dadi say she wished on Sunday?
qa.a: That she had fought to finish Class 10 instead of keeping quiet.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel hearing Dadi's regret?
qa.a: She was moved and thoughtful, noticing Dadi's voice didn't laugh, and chose to treat the regret as a map rather than a weight on her.

qa.q: Which risks does Ankita choose, and why does she skip others?
qa.a: She signs up for the English debate and plans to ask Professor Rao about the project, but won't skip sleep for marks, because only some risks will give her future self peace.

qa.q: How might Jyoti Dadi feel reading this letter?
qa.a: She may feel relieved that her words helped instead of burdened, and proud that her story is shaping her granddaughter's choices 🙂

grounding: A young woman hears her grandmother's regret about not studying and treats it as a warning, choosing which risks now are worth her future peace.

passage: Vinita, you know my Nana, the one who fixes every radio in our lane? Last month, while I was holding the torch for him, he went quiet and said, "I was good at maths, Rafiq. My father needed a hand at the shop, and I never asked if I could stay in school. I still dream about that exam hall." Honestly, my first thought was panic, like now I have to be brilliant for both of us. Then I watched him laugh at the next radio, and I thought, no, he isn't handing me a debt. He's handing me a warning. So I sorted things. Asking my professor for the lab assistant post, even if I'm rejected: worth it. Raising my hand when the group ignores my idea: worth it. Dropping out to chase something on a whim: not worth it. I want to be an old man who fixes radios and doesn't dream about exam halls.

qa.q: What did Rafiq's Nana say he still dreams about?
qa.a: That exam hall.

qa.q: What was Rafiq's first thought when Nana shared the regret, and how did it change?
qa.a: He panicked, feeling he had to be brilliant for both of them, but then saw Nana was handing him a warning, not a debt.

qa.q: How does Rafiq decide which risks are worth taking?
qa.a: He asks which ones his older self would be glad of, so he goes for the lab post and speaking up, but not dropping out on a whim.

qa.q: What might it have cost Nana to say this to Rafiq?
qa.a: Admitting an old regret may have felt painful and exposing; seeing Rafiq take it well could bring him some peace.

grounding: A young man hears his grandfather regret leaving school and takes it as a warning rather than a burden, weighing which risks now are worth his future peace.

passage: I'm Kashish, Sachin's younger sister, and I was on the charpai when it happened. Dadaji was shelling peas and said, out of nowhere, "I should have told my father I wanted to be a teacher. I kept quiet, and I drove a truck for forty years." Sachin stopped scrolling. He didn't say anything. He just helped with the peas until the bowl was full, which he never does. That night his light stayed on late. The next week he told Papa, calmly, that he wanted to take the B.Ed entrance along with his final year, not instead of it. I don't know exactly what went on in his head. But when he left for the exam, he touched Dadaji's feet for longer than usual, and Dadaji patted his cheek twice.

qa.q: What job did Dadaji do for forty years?
qa.a: He drove a truck.

qa.q: What might Sachin helping with the peas until the bowl was full suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: He seemed moved and thoughtful, perhaps wanting to stay close to Dadaji while taking in the regret, though Kashish can't be sure.

qa.q: Why was taking the B.Ed entrance alongside his final year a sensible choice?
qa.a: It acted on Dadaji's lesson without throwing away his degree, a risk worth taking so he won't carry the same silence later.

qa.q: How might Dadaji have felt when Sachin touched his feet before the exam?
qa.a: He may have felt his regret had turned into something useful, and felt proud and comforted, as the two pats on the cheek suggest.

grounding: A sister watches her brother hear their grandfather's regret about staying silent and quietly act on it as a warning, not a burden.

passage:
Sunday. Ankita, twenty, was oiling Kamla Nani's hair on the balcony when Nani said quietly, "My sister and I stopped speaking in 1987 over a gold chain. I always meant to say sorry first. Then she died. I wish I had opened my mouth." Ankita's hands stopped. The words sat on her chest all evening like a stone.
Thursday. In the hostel Ankita reread a draft she had kept for a month: an email to Professor Rao asking to join his river-survey project. She had been too shy to send it. She thought of Nani's voice. Not a weight, she decided. A warning. Which silence would bother her at seventy?
Two weeks later. She had sent it and got an interview. That evening she phoned Nani. "You made me brave." Nani laughed. "Good. Someone should use my mistakes."

qa.q: What did Nani and her sister stop speaking over?
qa.a: They stopped speaking over a gold chain.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel on Sunday after Nani's words, and how had that changed by Thursday?
qa.a: At first she felt weighed down, as if the words sat on her chest like a stone; by Thursday she felt braver, taking them as a warning, not a weight.

qa.q: What choice did Ankita make at the turning point on Thursday?
qa.a: She asked herself which silence would bother her at seventy, and decided to send the email to Professor Rao she had been too shy to send.

qa.q: How might Nani feel hearing 'You made me brave'?
qa.a: She may feel some peace, since her regret has helped Ankita, which is why she laughs and says someone should use her mistakes.

grounding: A young woman hears her grandmother's regret about staying silent, takes it as a warning rather than a burden, and chooses a risk her future self will be glad of.

passage:
"Tushar, my boy, you've been quiet since I told you about the nursing school. Don't carry it for me.
I was sixteen, and the nurses at the district hospital said I had good hands and could train. My father said a girl from our house does not go and live in a hostel. I didn't say one word back. I married at eighteen, and I've been happy enough, beta. But when your cousin qualified last year, I cried in the kitchen.
Now you're twenty-one, thinking of saying no to the Pune fellowship because your mother will worry. I'm not telling you to go. I'm telling you to ask one question: at my age, which choice will let you sit in peace?
You're nodding the way your grandfather did when he had made up his mind. Good. Go and phone them. Your Ganga Dadi will be right here."

qa.q: What did the nurses at the district hospital tell Dadi when she was sixteen?
qa.a: That she had good hands and could train.

qa.q: Why does Dadi tell Tushar not to carry it for her?
qa.a: She sees he has gone quiet and heavy with her regret, and she wants it to guide him, not burden him.

qa.q: What question does Dadi give Tushar for his choice about the Pune fellowship?
qa.a: At her age, which choice will let him sit in peace, rather than simply avoiding his mother's worry.

qa.q: Why might Dadi have cried in the kitchen when the cousin qualified?
qa.a: Seeing the cousin qualify reminded her of the training she never spoke up for, stirring old regret alongside her pride.

grounding: A grandmother shares her regret about not speaking up for nurse training, and her grandson takes it as guidance for a risk worth his future peace.
